**Where we are ahead:** the only Zig traceroute engine found; against the C tools it is a testable library with an injectable transport (offline canned-packet tests on a virtual clock), partial-trace-on-transport-failure, spoof hardening (Echo Reply must come from the destination; random ident/seq; bounded run time), and it returns a structured `Trace`. **Where we are behind** (re-checked 2026-10-04): no TCP method, sequential probing only (slow on dark hops), no ECMP-aware (Paris/Dublin) strategy; ASN/reverse-DNS annotation is left to sibling modules (`dns`) (→ Backlog). Built since the survey: the UDP method, RFC 4884/4950 MPLS label stacks, interface/source/TOS/fwmark.

## Design & invariants
Pure engine behind a `Transport` seam: `traceWith` is the hop state machine over an injectable
transport (`sendFn` with TTL / `recvFn` bytes + source / `nowFn` clock), fully offline-testable from
canned packet bytes on a virtual clock; `LinuxTransport` + `trace` are the live path. Correlation over
a bounded flat slot scheme: each probe's wire sequence is `seq_base +% slot` (slot =
hop·probes_per_hop + probe); a response — even one arriving after its probe already timed out — maps
back to its slot via the ident/seq quoted inside the ICMP error (parsed by `icmp.echo.parseV4/V6`),
so late replies land in the right hop. One probe in flight by default: no router sees a burst and every
RTT is unambiguous. `Options.parallel` opens a window (traceroute(8)'s `-N`, whose default is 16): a probe
goes when fewer than that are unanswered and within their deadline and `send_gap_ms` has passed, an answer
past its deadline still lands in its slot but frees no second place, and the trace ends at the LOWEST
terminal TTL, whichever arrived first; answers above it are not in the result. With `parallel = 1` this is
the same engine: the 24 kernel-oracle transcripts replay unchanged. `max_silent_hops` is mtr's `-U`. Hop count and probes-per-hop are bounded
(`Options.validate`; `max_probes_per_hop = 16`, `max_payload = 1024`). Allocation: `Trace` owns
exactly two slices (`hops`, `probes`), sized to the used prefix and freed by `deinit`; per-hop
`stats()` streams through a `latency-stats` Accumulator. Live path is Linux: a raw ICMP socket
(CAP_NET_RAW) or, for the ICMP method, an unprivileged ping socket (`SocketKind`, `.auto` = raw
when permitted, else ping) — see "Unprivileged traceroute" below; per-probe TTL via setsockopt
IP_TTL/IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS; ppoll for the timeout.
Clean-room from the classic traceroute(8)/mtr ICMP method (Van Jacobson's TTL-stepping applied to
ICMP Echo — a public technique) and RFC 792 ICMP formats via the sibling `icmp.echo` codec — see
README Provenance.

### A transport failure returns a partial `Trace`, not just an error

`traceWith` used to propagate a `sendFn`/`recvFn` failure with `try`, which discarded every
hop already collected — for a traceroute, eight good hops then a broken socket is most of the
answer, not a failure to report as opaquely as a caller mistake. Zig has no error payloads, so
carrying the partial result out alongside the error needed a shape decision:

- **Considered and rejected: an out-parameter** (`traceWith(gpa, t, dest, opts, partial: ?*Trace)`).
  Works, but it is a second way to receive a `Trace` bolted onto the existing one, and every
  caller — including every offline test in this file — would need to thread a pointer through
  whether or not it cares.
- **Considered and rejected: split the return into `struct { trace: Trace, err: ?TransportError }`
  with no Zig error at all.** This erases the real distinction between "a partial trace, because
  the transport broke mid-run" and "no trace at all, because `Options` were invalid or the initial
  allocation failed" — `InvalidOptions`/`OutOfMemory` happen before a single probe is sent, so
  there is nothing to hand back for them, and forcing every caller to unwrap a `Trace` value for
  those cases too would manufacture a fake one.
- **Chosen: extend `Trace` with a `transport_err: ?TransportError` field, and narrow `TraceError`
  to `error{ InvalidOptions, OutOfMemory }`.** This follows the module's own existing shape:
  `Trace` already records *how* a trace stopped as data (`reached`, `unreachable_code`), not as a
  distinct error per termination mode — a transport failure is simply a third way to stop early,
  and was the odd one out for using the `!` channel instead of a field. `sendFn`/`recvFn` failures
  are now caught inside `traceWith` (`catch |err| { transport_err = err; break :outer; }`) instead
  of propagated with `try`, so the function falls through to the same hop-packing code every other
  termination path already uses, and returns a `Trace` whose `hops`/`probes` hold whatever was
  collected up to the failure. The genuine no-partial-data cases (`InvalidOptions`, the initial
  `gpa.alloc` before any probe exists) keep the ordinary Zig error channel — nothing to carry
  alongside them either way.

**`hops_used` on a send failure.** A failure on a hop's first probe (`pi == 0`) means nothing
about that hop was ever attempted, so it is excluded from `hops_used` (set to `hi`, not `hi + 1`)
— otherwise the returned `Trace` would contain a hop whose every probe reads `.timeout` despite
none of them having been sent, indistinguishable from a hop that really was probed and got no
answer. A failure on a *later* probe of the same hop (or any `recvFn` failure, which by
definition follows a successful send) leaves `hops_used` as already set — that hop did get at
least one real attempt, the same way an `unreachable_code` stop mid-hop keeps the hop it stopped
in (see `wire.zig`'s sibling test "destination unreachable terminates and records the code").

**BREAKING for a caller that matched `TraceError`/`TransportError` on `traceWith`'s return.** A
`try traceWith(...)` or `catch |err| switch (err) { error.SendFailed, error.RecvFailed => ... }`
no longer compiles/fires for those two — the same failure now arrives as `tr.transport_err` on a
successful return. See CHANGELOG.md.

## UDP method, extensions, live options (2026-10-04)

**UDP.** Probe *k* is a datagram from the transport's bound source port (`Options.ident`, the
correlation token — the live path uses the kernel's ephemeral port, or `Options.source_port`) to `udp_port_base + k`; the
`validate` rule keeps that window inside 1…65535. A reply is an ICMP error quoting an IPv4/IPv6
header with protocol/next-header 17 and the probe's source and destination ports, with the
quoted destination equal to the trace's (the A1 F3 rule, now also for UDP). The destination's
own Port Unreachable (IPv4 code 3, IPv6 code 4) from the destination's address is `.reply` and
sets `reached`; any other Destination Unreachable — or a Port Unreachable from anyone else (A1
F1) — is terminal. The same first-answer-wins rule (A1 F12) holds. The live path sends from a
UDP socket and receives on the same raw ICMP socket as the ICMP method; a send that fails with a
pending ICMP-induced socket error (ECONNREFUSED etc., which belongs to the previous probe) is
retried once.

**Extensions (RFC 4884) and MPLS (RFC 4950).** The ICMPv4 length field (byte 5, 32-bit words;
ICMPv6 byte 4, 64-bit words) locates the extension after an original datagram of at least 128
bytes; a router predating RFC 4884 puts it at 128 bytes with the field 0, accepted only with a
version-2 header and a non-zero, verifying checksum (a zero checksum means "not computed", which
is fine only when the length field already proved an extension is there). Objects are walked by
length; class 1 / C-Type 1 entries become `MplsEntry` (label 20 bits, TC 3, S 1, TTL 8), at most
`max_mpls_labels` per probe. ICMPv4 checksums are verified before any of this (`icmpMessage`),
as `icmp.echo` does for the ICMP method.

**Interface Information (RFC 5837, 2026-11-02).** `ifInfoOf(family, msg)` walks the same objects
for class 2 and returns an `IfInfoSet` (`Probe.if_info`, filled by `classifyIcmp`; at most
`max_if_infos` = 4, one per role, §4.5). The C-Type is read most significant bit first (§4.1):
bits 0-1 the role (`IfRole`: incoming, sub-IP, outgoing, next hop), bits 2-3 reserved and
ignored, then `0x08` ifIndex, `0x04` address, `0x02` name, `0x01` MTU, whose fields follow in
that order: ifIndex (4 octets), address sub-object (AFI 1 or 2, 2 reserved octets, 4 or 16
octets), name sub-object (a length octet that counts itself, a multiple of 4 up to 64, NUL
padded: a name of up to `max_if_name` = 63), MTU (4 octets). A damaged object (a field past its
object, bytes left over, a bad name length, an AFI that is unknown or not the message's family)
ends the walk and keeps the objects before it; two objects of one role are illegal and drop the
whole set. An all-padding name reads as "no name". `Probe` carries the set inline: `@sizeOf(Probe)`
grew from 112 to 512 bytes. Anchored on `golang.org/x/net/icmp` v0.61.0 (`tools/go_oracle`, 136
frozen messages in `src/if_info_vectors.zig`: every role and every subset of the four fields,
both families, Time Exceeded and Destination Unreachable, several objects, MPLS ahead of the
object). x/net agrees with the RFC on the bit values and field order; it can only marshal a name
or an MTU together with an ifIndex (the other subsets are encoded by hand from §4 and parsed by
x/net), copies a name longer than 63 octets past its sub-object, and its parser skips an unknown
AFI without consuming the address — none of which this decoder copies.

**Live options.** `iface` → SO_BINDTODEVICE on both sockets, `source` → bind (raw socket via
`icmp.Socket`, UDP socket directly), `tos` → IP_TOS / IPV6_TCLASS on the socket that sends,
`fwmark` → SO_MARK. A live test reads them back with `getsockopt`.

## Continuous mode over UDP and TCP (2026-11-02)

`MtrOptions.method` with `udp_port_base`, `dst_port`, `flow_stable`, `payload_fill`, for `Mtr` and `MtrSet`
alike: all of them go through the same `Prober` as `traceWith`, so there is no second copy of the
method-specific code. A round spends a window of wire ids, as ICMP always did: classic UDP moves up through
ports (`validate` wants two of the largest windows above `udp_port_base`), flow-stable moves the id in the
checksum. Over UDP, `flow_stable` is what one wants here, and it is not the default only so that a field
left alone keeps today's behaviour: classic ports change between rounds, so behind a per-flow balancer the
path flaps. TCP has no flow-stable form here: a round has several attempts open, so the source port is
the kernel's and `source_port` is refused. A set's members can leave with different source addresses, so
for flow-stable UDP each member asks once (`Transport.flowSourceFn`). `max_unknown` is mtr's `-U`.

`LinuxTransport` keeps `2 x max_parallel` TCP attempts: a set probing many silent TTLs closes the oldest after
that many further sends, about 640 ms at the default gap, and a silent hop had nothing to say anyway.

Oracle: `mtr-*` and `mtrset-*` in `tools/kernel_oracle.py` run `LiveMtr` and `LiveMtrSet` on the live chain,
every method, against the topology, and `mtr -r` agrees for ICMP, UDP and TCP.

## TCP method (2026-11-02)

A connection attempt per probe, non-blocking, with the probe's TTL and `IP_RECVERR`: traceroute(8)'s
`tcpconn` shape, not half-open raw SYN. It needs no privilege, which is what zpinger runs with, and the
kernel matches any ICMP error to the connection by its quoted sequence number before queueing it, a
stronger check than the 16 bits the other methods have. The cost: on an open port the handshake
completes, so the application behind it sees a connection (reset at once: `SO_LINGER` 0, no
TIME_WAIT on our side). Half-open raw SYN stays in the Backlog; the result would be the same.

The socket identifies the probe, so no packet is parsed: `Transport.sendTcpFn` / `recvTcpFn` deal in
`TcpEvent`s. Measured in namespaces before writing it (2026-11-02, Linux 7.0): a Time Exceeded on a
SYN_SENT socket arrives on the error queue with the router as offender, v4 and v6; so does a filter's
Destination Unreachable; an RST reads `ECONNREFUSED` from `SO_ERROR` with the queue empty; a SYN-ACK is
`POLLOUT` with no error. `TCP_SYNCNT` 1 keeps a silent hop from retransmitting six more times.
`LinuxTransport` keeps up to `2 x max_parallel` attempts open, so an answer past its deadline can still
land, and closes the oldest when it needs the place; `Options.iface` must outlive the transport here,
because each attempt opens a socket. A fixed `source_port` is one 4-tuple, so one attempt at a time.

`Probe.code` of a `.reply` says which: `tcp_syn_ack`, `tcp_rst`. Oracle: `tcp` in
`tools/kernel_oracle.py`, the four scenarios plus `open-port` (a listener on the server), against
`traceroute -T`.

## Flow-stable probes (Paris traceroute, 2026-11-02)

Per-flow load balancers hash the 5-tuple, so classic UDP probes, whose destination port differs, can
take different branches and draw a path no packet took. `Options.flow_stable` keeps what they hash
constant and carries the probe id where they do not look.

- **UDP:** one destination port. The id is in the payload's second word, and the first word is solved
  so that the UDP checksum equals the id as well (RFC 1071; the pseudo-header needs the source address,
  `Transport.flow_source`, which `LinuxTransport` gets from a connected throwaway socket). An answer
  yields the id from the quoted payload when the quote reaches it, else from the quoted checksum. The
  order was forced by the oracle: on a `veth` with offload the first router quotes a checksum nobody has
  computed yet, and a NAT rewrites it. The error-queue path never sees the UDP header, so there the
  payload copy is all there is, and a router quoting only the 8 bytes RFC 792 asks for leaves a `*`.
- **ICMP:** the sequence number varies and the identifier compensates, so that the ICMP checksum, which
  is all a balancer can hash of an Echo Request, is constant. A ping socket rewrites the identifier, so
  the combination is refused. Linux's own multipath hash ignores ICMP fields, so this variant has no
  ECMP oracle: the replay holds the bytes and the checksum test holds the arithmetic.
- **Oracle:** `ecmp` in `tools/kernel_oracle.py`, a router balancing by the 5-tuple
  (`fib_multipath_hash_policy=1`). Classic UDP shows both next hops at that TTL, flow-stable shows one
  (raw and error-queue paths); with offload off, every quoted checksum is the id, so the arithmetic
  agrees with the kernel's.
- **`Hop.distinctAddresses` on a flow-stable trace** means per-packet balancing, not per-flow.

## Unprivileged UDP: the UDP socket's own error queue (2026-11-02)

`.udp` with `.dgram`, or with `.auto` when a raw socket is refused, as traceroute(8) runs without
privilege. `sock` is the UDP socket itself and only its error queue is read: a datagram on that socket
comes from anyone and is never an answer, so it is read and dropped (left unread it would keep the
poll from sleeping). The kernel returns the datagram's payload, not its header, so `errQueuePacket`
rebuilds the quoted UDP header from the socket's port and `msg_name`'s and hands the engine the same
message a raw socket sees: one parser, the same spoof rules. Oracle: 8 more kernel transcripts
(`udp-dgram`), every hop as the topology dictates and as traceroute(8) reports it.

## Unprivileged traceroute: the ping socket's error queue (2026-10-31)

The claim this SPEC used to make — "DGRAM sockets deliver ICMP errors on the error queue, not as
packets, so raw is required" — was half right: they do arrive only on the error queue, but that
queue carries everything a hop needs. With IP_RECVERR/IPV6_RECVERR (set by `icmp.Socket.open`) a
Time Exceeded or Destination Unreachable about one of the socket's echo requests is queued as
`sock_extended_err` (ICMP type, code, origin), the reporting router as `SO_EE_OFFENDER`, the
probe's destination as `msg_name`, and the quoted echo header (ident, seq) as payload —
`icmp.Socket.recvErr` now returns all four (`ErrInfo.offender`, `.origin`). The kernel delivers
these per socket by echo ident, so only the socket's own probes reach it; the ident is the
kernel's (it rewrites what we write), which is why `trace` uses `lt.ident()` there.

**Design: rebuild the raw socket's packet, keep one parser.** `LinuxTransport.recvImpl` on a ping
socket reads the normal queue (Echo Replies, without IP header) and the error queue; each ICMP
entry becomes the RFC 792 / RFC 4443 message a raw socket would have delivered
(`errQueuePacket`: type/code, a quoted IPv4/IPv6 header whose destination is `msg_name`, the
quoted echo header; an IPv4 checksum computed over it) with `from` = the offender. The engine
then applies exactly the raw path's rules — ident, slot, first answer wins, quoted destination
must be `dest` (A1 F1/F3/F12) — through the same `classifyIcmp`. Considered and rejected: a
second classification path for "already decoded" answers — two places to keep the spoof rules in
step for no gain, while the rebuild is 40 lines and its output is checked by the same parser.
A local error (`SO_EE_ORIGIN_LOCAL`, e.g. EMSGSIZE) carries no ICMP message and is dropped.

**What a ping socket cannot do:** the ICMP extension objects (RFC 4884/4950) are not on the error
queue, so `Probe.mpls` stays empty; the UDP method needs a socket that sees ICMP about UDP
datagrams; the UDP method without privilege reads its own UDP socket instead (below). `.auto` tries raw first.

**How it is shown:** the kernel oracle runs every scenario a third time as `icmp-dgram` (8 traces, v4 and
v6: clean, a silent router, Administratively Prohibited, a silent server) — each hop the
topology's router, the same as the raw traces and traceroute(8); the replay test feeds the
rebuilt packets through `traceWith`. A live test traces 127.0.0.1 over a ping socket in the netns
lane, where `ping_group_range` is open and no capability is held.

## Continuous mode: `Mtr` (2026-10-31)

What mtr shows, as a library: `Mtr.round` sends one ICMP probe to every TTL of the path (`gap_ms`
apart — a paced round, never a burst), waits `timeout_ms` after the last, and folds the answers
into `MtrHop` running statistics (sent, received → loss, last/best/worst/avg RTT, jitter = mean
|ΔRTT| between consecutive answers, the responders seen — several mean a load-balanced hop, the
last Destination Unreachable code). `LiveMtr` is the same over its own `LinuxTransport`, so it
works unprivileged on a ping socket.

**More statistics (2026-11-02).** `MtrHop` also keeps mtr's remaining columns, all updated in
`record` and all plain data. `worst_jitter_ns` is the largest |ΔRTT|. `interarrival_jitter_ns` is the
RFC 3550 A.8 estimator J += (|D| − J)/16 over consecutive answers, in integer ns (the division
truncates; the bias stays under 16 ns, and the tests hold it to that against a float filter).
`stddevNs()` is the sample (n − 1) standard deviation, null below two answers, computed exactly:
n·Σx² − (Σx)² in 256-bit integers from the saturating `sum_ns` and a saturating u128 `sumsq_ns2`
(an RTT is at most `max_mtr_timeout_ms`, 2^34 ns, so its square is under 2^68 and a u32 count of
squares cannot overflow 2^128), then an integer square root floored to a whole ns. There is no
Welford state and no float subtraction, so a 1 µs spread on a 100 ms mean does not cancel away.
`geomeanNs()` is exp of the mean of ln(RTT) kept in `sum_ln_ns` (f64; an RTT of 0 counts as 1 ns),
null with no answer. `@sizeOf(MtrHop)` grew from 168 to 208 bytes.

**Invariants.** (1) *Rate:* `round` itself waits out the rest of `interval_ms` since the previous
round began, and `validate` floors `interval_ms` at `min_mtr_interval_ms` (100) and caps
`timeout_ms`, `gap_ms`, `payload_size` — a caller looping on `round` cannot probe faster than one
round per interval, whatever it does. (2) *One RTT per probe:* round r's probes carry the sequence
window `seq_base + r·hop_count …`; an answer is taken only inside its own round, so a late answer
(past `timeout_ms`) quotes a finished window and is dropped — it is a loss, never a sample of a
later probe. (3) *Same answer rules as `traceWith`* (`classifyIcmp`): ident, quoted destination,
Echo Reply only from `dest`, first answer per probe wins. (4) *Path end:* the first TTL answered
by the destination (or a Destination Unreachable) ends the path; later rounds probe up to it
only. A shorter path forgets the TTLs beyond it; a router answering at the end TTL (the path
grew) sends probing back to `max_hops`. (5) A transport error aborts the round uncounted. Memory:
four slices sized `max_hops − first_ttl + 1`, allocated by `init`, nothing per round.

Considered and rejected: carrying unanswered probes into the next round (mtr counts late replies
in some builds) — it makes "which probe was this RTT" ambiguous and the loss figure depend on the
interval; a separate thread or `std.Io` inside the engine — the caller owns scheduling, a round
is a bounded blocking call over the same `Transport` seam, offline-testable on a virtual clock.

## Many destinations: `MtrSet` (2026-10-31)

**Why.** A consumer that runs several live traces (zpinger: one per watched host) used to run one
`LiveMtr` each: every trace probed its own TTL 1, 2, … — the same home gateway and ISP routers —
once a second. Routers limit the ICMP errors they generate per source (Linux: `icmp_ratelimit`,
about one Time Exceeded a second, with a small burst; hardware routers police their control plane
similarly), so N traces across one router made it refuse most of them: false loss at exactly the
hops every trace shares. `MtrSet` probes such a hop once per round, whatever the number of traces.

**Design.** One transport per family; a probe goes to its member's destination through the new
`Transport.sendToFn` (a raw or ping socket is unconnected: `sendto` per packet). A round plans who
probes which TTL, sends TTL by TTL across members `gap_ms` apart, collects until `timeout_ms` after
the last, copies each shared TTL's answer to its sharers, and hands every member its answers via
`Mtr.finishRound` — the same bookkeeping `Mtr.round` uses, so path end, reset and statistics behave
identically. Sequence numbers: slot i of round r is `seq_base + r·(max_set_members·hop_count) + i`
(≤ 4080 per window, so windows never overlap); an answer's quoted sequence picks the slot, and then
`classifyIcmp` checks it against *that* probe's destination — the spoof rules (ident, quoted
destination, Echo Reply only from the destination, first answer wins) are `Mtr`'s.

**Sharing rule.** Per member and TTL the set keeps the router answering there and its run of
answers (a different router restarts the run; a lost probe does not). Two members share the leading
TTLs where (1) each probed the TTL `settle_rounds` times and (2) no two different routers answered
them there, cut back to the last TTL where both *settled* (`settle_rounds` answers in a row) on the
same router. Hence: a silent hop between agreeing routers is shared, a trailing one is not; and a
router that answers one member and never the other — the rate-limited router this exists for — is
shared once the routers after it agree. Member i takes a TTL from the lowest j < i that shares it
*and probes it itself*: "does not contradict" is not transitive across a silent hop, so the copy
always comes from a real probe of a member that agrees with i. Every member probes its whole path
itself once in `verify_every` rounds (staggered by index); a different router there restarts its run
and ends sharing from that TTL. Considered and rejected: sharing on a single matching answer (an
ECMP balancer hashing on the destination gives two members different routers at the same TTL only
some of the time), and requiring an answer on both sides (the rate-limited router never answers the
second member, so it would never be shared — measured in the test with a once-a-second router: no
sharing at all).

**What it does not do.** A router that appears in two different branches (different TTL prefixes)
still gets one probe per branch. The copied answer's RTT is the owner's; it is the same router at
the same TTL over a path both members agree on up to that TTL. Members of one family only (a
consumer runs one set per family). Single owner: add/remove between rounds.

## Threat model / out of scope
The live trace needs CAP_NET_RAW (raw ICMP socket) or, for the ICMP method, a group inside
`net.ipv4.ping_group_range` (ping socket). On a ping socket the kernel only delivers answers about
the socket's own echo identifier — a narrower intake than a raw socket's, and the same engine
rules apply on top. Responses are **not authenticated**: only
ident/seq quoted in the ICMP error are checked, so a spoofed router response with the right ident/seq
would be attributed to a hop (path measurement, not authentication); a response quoting a slot not
yet sent, or a slot that already has an answer, is rejected as a spoof/duplicate (A1 F5/F12 — first
non-timeout write wins a slot, not last). An Echo Reply additionally must carry the destination's own
source address to complete the trace (`reached = true`) — A1 F1: without that check, a single spoofed
Echo Reply with the right ident/seq from ANY address truncated the whole trace to one hop attributed
to the spoofer, which is a stronger claim than "path measurement" and is what the `reached` field's
own doc comment promises. `trace()` draws a fresh random ident and starting sequence per call via
`getrandom(2)` (A1 F2) rather than the raw socket's PID-derived identifier and the fixed default
`seq_base = 1` — this raises the bar against a *blind off-path* spoofer to a full unknown 16+16 bits;
it does nothing against an on-path attacker, who reads the real values off the wire. `Options.validate`
also bounds the worst-case wall time of a whole run, not just each field individually (A1 F6/F8 —
`max_run_ms`), since `max_hops`/`probes_per_hop`/`timeout_ms` each being individually bounded still
let the worst legal combination run for ~202,817 days and put ~4.2 MB on the wire toward one address
with no rate limit. Malformed/hostile ICMP bytes never panic — anything unrecognized is `.ignored` and
the probe falls through to a clean timeout (`*`); a corpus-seeded `testing.fuzz` test exercises this
directly (A1 F9).

**No destination validation (A1 F7, by design, not by oversight).** `trace`/`traceWith` accept and
probe whatever `netaddr.Ip` they are given — loopback, link-local (including the `169.254.169.254`
cloud-metadata address), private, unspecified (`0.0.0.0`) and multicast/broadcast destinations are
all accepted and probed. `netaddr` is a declared dependency and exports `isLoopback`,
`isLinkLocalUnicast`, `isPrivate`, `isMulticast`, `isUnspecified`; this module calls none of them.
For a diagnostic tool, tracing to a link-local next hop or a private-range destination is normal,
legitimate use — the previous absence of a documented stance (not the absence of the checks
themselves) was the actual gap. **A caller that exposes `trace`/`traceWith` to a destination chosen
by an untrusted party (the SSRF-shaped case) must apply its own `netaddr`-predicate validation before
calling in** — this module will not do it for them.

**Quoted-header and checksum checks.** `icmp.echo.Reply.icmp_error` carries the quoted datagram's
declared source, destination and protocol (`quoted_src`/`quoted_dst`/`quoted_proto`, A1 F2), and the ICMPv4
checksum is verified before a message is used (`icmpMessage`, as `icmp.echo.parseV4` does); ICMPv6's checksum
needs the pseudo-header, which only the kernel has. These are `icmp` module findings (`icmp`'s F2/F7 — A1
audit) shared with `pathmtu` and `icmp`'s own `Pinger`. Out of scope:
non-Linux live path, MTU/PMTU discovery.

## Verification
Offline-first: the hop state machine runs against a fake transport that builds canned RFC 792-shaped
response bytes (Time Exceeded, Echo Reply, Destination Unreachable, drops, late replies, load-
balanced hops, malformed/hostile input) through the real `icmp.echo` parsers on a deterministic
virtual clock — TTL/ident/seq stamping, terminal-code handling, `*` timeouts, `distinctAddresses`,
per-hop `latency-stats`, IPv4 raw-header shape, IPv6, option validation. One live test traces
`127.0.0.1`, skipped without CAP_NET_RAW. Run: `zig build test-traceroute`.

**2026-10-04:** real kernel replies to UDP probes from a veth router sandbox (client → router →
server in three throwaway netns inside `unshare -rnm`, tcpdump-decoded): the router's Time
Exceeded and the server's Port Unreachable drive a two-hop UDP trace to `reached`; the same bytes
are refused under a wrong source port, a port window that excludes them, a different destination,
a quoted protocol other than UDP and a damaged ICMP checksum; the server's Port Unreachable from
the router's address is terminal, not `reached`; a late duplicate does not overwrite a slot. An
MPLS-extended Time Exceeded that tcpdump decodes ("checksum … (correct)", "label 16, tc 0, ttl 1")
yields its two-entry stack; each RFC 4884 rule (128-byte minimum, version 2, C-Type 1, the
compatibility checksum) is shown rejecting on its own with every checksum valid. IPv6 UDP uses
code 4. Live (CAP_NET_RAW): a UDP trace to 127.0.0.1 ends on the loopback's Port Unreachable,
and `iface`/`source`/`tos` are read back off the sockets. Mutation 2026-10-04: 29 mutants, all
killed.

## Backlog / deferred
- **2026-10-31 (no-panic sweep GX, fix round):** `LinuxTransport.recvImpl` used to busy-spin after the first ICMP error (the queued IP_RECVERR entry keeps POLLERR set); it now drains the error queue after each wakeup (`waitForData`) and discards the entries (a raw socket also gets the message as a datagram). A forged Destination Unreachable / Time Exceeded with the right ident/seq/quoted destination is accepted (documented threat model above, unchanged).
Documented out-of-scope: non-Linux live path, MTU/PMTU discovery.
- **2026-10-04:** UDP method, ICMP extensions/MPLS and source/interface/TOS are **done** (see
  "UDP method, extensions, live options"). Still deferred: **TCP** (needs SYN probes on a raw TCP
  socket or connect()-per-probe, and RST/SYN-ACK matching — a separate receive path; no consumer
  asks), **Paris/Dublin** (flow-stable UDP needs a constant 5-tuple, i.e. the
  probe id carried in the checksum/payload — builds on the UDP method, now possible). RFC 5837
  interface-information objects: DONE 2026-11-02 (see "Extensions (RFC 4884) and MPLS (RFC 4950)").
- **UDP and TCP probe methods** (survey 2026-09-30; UDP done 2026-10-04, TCP still open): traceroute(8)'s default is UDP and it offers TCP; trippy does ICMP/UDP/TCP. A user behind a firewall that drops ICMP echo gets a wall of `*`. Effort: medium (per-method probe encoding and matching the quoted transport header; the SPEC notes the quoted header is currently discarded by `icmp.echo`). Fits CONVENTIONS §2 (raw sockets via `std.os.linux`).
- **Multipath-aware strategy (Paris/Dublin-style flow-stable probes)** (survey 2026-09-30): per-flow load balancers make classic traceroute show false paths; trippy implements the two strategies. Effort: medium-large, depends on the UDP/TCP methods above. Fits §2.
- ~~**ICMP extension objects / MPLS labels (RFC 4884/4950)**~~ — DONE 2026-10-04 (survey 2026-09-30): traceroute(8) prints them *(inferred)*; needs the quoted-datagram parsing that `icmp.echo` currently drops. Effort: medium, partly in `icmp`. Fits §2.
- ~~**Source-address / interface / TOS options on the live path**~~ — DONE 2026-10-04 (survey 2026-09-30): multi-homed hosts cannot pick the egress; `icmp.Pinger` has `iface`/`oiface`/`tos`. Effort: small. Fits §2.

## Status
`gap · linux · client · single_owner` + deps: `icmp`, `netaddr`, `latency-stats` — canonical source
is `pub const meta` in src/root.zig.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — every path's expected values come from an implementation that is not ours.

**What the tests actually contain.** src/kernel_oracle_test.zig replays 16 live traces against real Linux routers (`tools/interop.zig` + `tools/kernel_oracle.py` → `kernel_oracle_vectors.zig`): a client → r1 → r2 → r3 → server chain of network namespaces per scenario — clean, r2 dropping its own Time Exceeded, r3 rejecting with Administratively Prohibited, the server dropping everything — for the ICMP and the UDP method over IPv4 and IPv6. The transport was recorded (every probe sent, every packet or timeout received, on a virtual clock); `traceWith` must send the same probes in the same order and report the same trace, and every hop is what the topology puts at that TTL — each router's client-side address, `*` for the silent one, `!X` (code 13 / v6 code 1) from the filter, the server's Echo Reply / Port Unreachable — which traceroute(8) 2.1.6 traced identically. The real tcpdump-decoded captures below anchor the refusal rules (wrong port, destination, protocol, checksum) and the RFC 4884/4950 extension parsing. Self only: the canned-fixture tests of hostile input, which have no outside answer

**Kernel oracle 2026-10-05.** One defect, fixed the same day: a terminal hop (Destination Unreachable) stopped after its first probe and reported the unsent rest as `.timeout` — a `*`, and a loss in `Hop.stats`, where traceroute(8) shows `!X` for every probe. It now sends the hop's full count, as it always did for the destination's hop.

**How it got there.** The anchoring work landed. DONE 466cc70: real 2-hop veth router; Time Exceeded from a real TTL decrement
